🎬 Opening — Why an Hour on Basics (3 min)

▼

Say this

“Before we touch your tenders, budgets or drawings, we're going to spend one hour on what this technology actually is. Not because it's hard — because people who understand why it works also understand when it fails. That's the difference between using AI and being fooled by it.”

Hands up — 30 seconds

  • Who has used ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot at least once?

1️⃣ What AI Is — and How It Differs from Normal Software (7 min)

▼
🎯 What we are trying to achieve

Feel the difference between rules a person writes and patterns a machine learns.

📦 What happens

Everyone votes on five cards; the last card shows the best systems mix both.

Normal software: rules written by people

Tally calculates GST because a programmer wrote the rule. Excel computes a total because someone wrote SUM. Same input, same output, every time — and it can only do what someone thought of.

Input → rules a person wrote → output

AI: rules learned from examples

Nobody writes the rule for “is this email spam?”. The system is shown millions of examples and learns the pattern itself. It can handle cases nobody anticipated — but it can also be wrong, and it can't always tell you why.

Examples → learned pattern → best guess

Words people use loosely — from widest to narrowest:

Artificial Intelligence
machines doing tasks that need judgement
⊃
Machine learning
learns patterns from data
⊃
Deep learning
very large “neural networks”
⊃
Generative AI
creates text, images, code
⊃
LLMs
ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot

Three families of AI you already meet

FamilyWhat it doesEveryday exampleAt Suroj
PredictiveForecasts or classifiesGoogle Maps arrival time; bank fraud alertsWhich cost head will overrun; which bid we'll win
GenerativeCreates new contentChatGPT writing an email; phone photo “magic eraser”Drafting an RFI, a pre-bid query, a monthly note
AgenticTakes steps towards a goal using toolsAn assistant that books a trip end to endReads every new drawing revision and flags slabs already poured

🗳️ 60-second room check — rule or learned?

GST = 18% of taxable value
Rule — a person wrote it once; it never changes on its own.
Your phone recognising your face
Learned — trained on many images; nobody wrote “if nose then…”.
Steel unit weight = d² ÷ 162
Rule — physics, written into the BBS sheet.
ChatGPT replying to a client email
Learned — patterns of language, not rules.
Spotting which invoices look like duplicates of each other
Can be either! Exact duplicates are a rule; “looks like a duplicate” is learned. Good AI work combines both.
🎤 Trainer: The last card is the point: the best results come from mixing hard rules (which AI should never guess) with learned judgement.

2️⃣ How an LLM Works — What Happens in the Back End (12 min)

▼
🎯 What we are trying to achieve

See, not just hear, that an LLM picks the next word by probability — and why answers vary.

📦 What happens

Watch the bars change with the temperature slider; type a sentence and see the tokens.

1 · Pre-training
reads a huge slice of the internet, books, code — learns to predict the next word
→
2 · Fine-tuning & feedback
people rate answers; it learns to be helpful, follow instructions, refuse harm
→
3 · Your chat (inference)
your words → tokens → predict the next token, again and again

1 · Pre-training — reading at enormous scale

The model reads trillions of words. At every position it guesses the next word, checks the real one, and nudges billions of internal numbers (“parameters”) to guess better next time. This takes months on thousands of specialised chips. What comes out is not a database of facts — it's a compressed sense of how language, facts and reasoning usually fit together.

2 · Fine-tuning — learning to be an assistant

A raw model just continues text. To make it answer questions, follow instructions and decline harmful requests, it is trained further on example conversations, and people rate its answers so it learns which ones are better. That's why ChatGPT and Claude sound like assistants and not like autocomplete.

3 · What happens when you press Enter

  1. Your text is split into tokens — chunks of words.
  2. The model looks at all the tokens together (this is the “transformer” — it weighs which words matter to which).
  3. It produces a probability for every possible next token.
  4. It picks one (usually a likely one, with a little randomness), adds it, and repeats — token by token — until the answer is done.

🔬 Live demo — next-word prediction

1.0

Illustrative probabilities, not from a real model. Low temperature → nearly always the top word. High → more variety, more odd answers. That's why the same question can get different answers.

🔬 Live demo — tokens

Approximate split for illustration — every model splits text slightly differently. Hindi and Marathi usually take more tokens than English for the same meaning.

Because it predicts, it…

BehaviourWhyWhat you do about it
Writes fluently in any styleIt has seen every styleTell it the tone, length and audience
Sounds confident when wrong (“hallucination”)A plausible next word isn't a checked factAsk for sources / clause / row; verify
Gives a different answer each timeThere's randomness in the pickingAsk for structure; regenerate and compare
Doesn't know your company, your tender, your budgetIt only knows what it read in training + what you give itAttach the document; give context
Doesn't know recent eventsTraining stops at a date (“knowledge cutoff”)Use web search mode for current facts
Gets long arithmetic wrong in its headDigits are predicted like wordsAsk it to calculate with code, or for the formula
Forgets things in a very long chat or huge fileIt can only hold so much at once (“context window”)Split the work; start a new chat per task

So how can it do real tasks?

Modern apps add tools around the model: reading uploaded files and images, searching the web, running code to calculate exactly, creating documents. When ChatGPT or Claude “analyses your spreadsheet”, the model is writing code and a computer runs it. That's why asking it to calculate beats asking it to guess.

“Is it thinking?”

Newer “reasoning” models write out intermediate steps before answering, which makes them much better at maths, logic and multi-step problems — and slower. It's still prediction underneath, just with a scratchpad. It has no beliefs, no stake in being right, and no accountability. You do.

🎤 Trainer: Analogy for the room: your phone's keyboard suggests the next word from your messages. An LLM is that idea after reading a library the size of the internet — and then being coached by thousands of people on how to be a good assistant.

3️⃣ The Tools — and Your First Three Prompts (8 min)

▼
🎯 What we are trying to achieve

Get everyone's first hands-on with an AI app, and catch it guessing.

📦 What happens

Three prompts in pairs: explain, draft, and one question it cannot know.

ToolMade byGood forNote
ChatGPTOpenAIAll-round: writing, analysis, images, voiceMost widely used
ClaudeAnthropicLong documents, careful analysis, writing, codeStrong at reading big files
GeminiGoogleWorks with Gmail, Docs, DriveGood if you live in Google
Microsoft CopilotMicrosoftInside Word, Excel, Outlook, TeamsWith a business licence, data stays in Microsoft 365
NotebookLMGoogleAnswers only from documents you upload, with referencesGood for big document sets

Same underlying idea, different strengths. Features, limits and prices change every few months — the habits in this hour don't.

Anatomy of the app

  • New chat — one task per chat; start fresh for a new topic
  • 📎 Attach — PDFs, spreadsheets, photos
  • Model picker — faster vs more thorough
  • Search / tools toggle — for current information
  • Edit / regenerate — fix your question, try again
  • Settings → data controls — turn off training on your chats

Free vs paid vs company accounts

  • Free — limits on files, usage and the best models
  • Paid personal — more capacity; still your personal account
  • Business / enterprise — admin controls and stronger data commitments; the right place for company work

Read the data terms of whichever plan you use.

📱 Your first three prompts — 5 minutes, in pairs

  1. Explain: “Explain [EMD / CPI / an RFI] in simple Hindi for a new site engineer, in 5 lines.”
  2. Draft: “Write a polite reminder to [a client / a project manager / the MEPF contractor] for a reply that is 5 days late. Under 80 words.” Then reply: “Make it firmer.”
  3. Test it: ask something it cannot know — “[What was L1 on our last tender? / What is P01's EAC? / How many sleeves are on L2?]”. Watch: does it say it doesn't know, ask you for data — or make something up?
🎤 Trainer: Use the swap table for the bracketed choices. Collect two answers to prompt 3 aloud — any invented answer is the perfect bridge to Module 6.

4️⃣ Prompting Basics — How to Ask (7 min)

▼
Role
who it should be
+
Task
exactly what to do
+
Context
the document, the situation
+
Format
table, length, language
+
Constraints
what not to do
+
Evidence
source / row / clause or NOT FOUND

Weak

“Write an email about the delay.”

Generic, wrong tone, invents details.

Strong

“You are a project coordinator at an Indian construction company. Write an email to the client's PMC explaining a 10-day delay in the roof slab due to late MEP drawings (received 18 June, slab planned 2 June). Polite, factual, under 120 words, end with a request for a meeting this week. Don't promise a new date.”

THE TEMPLATE — SAVE IT IN YOUR PHONE NOTES
Role: You are a [job] at an Indian construction company. Task: [one clear job] Context: [what the attached file is / the situation / the date] Format: [table / bullets / email; length; language] Constraints: Use only what I give you. Don't invent facts. Evidence: For every fact, give the source (clause, row, page). If it isn't there, write NOT FOUND.

Five habits that matter more than clever wording

  • Give it the material — it can't read your mind or your files unless you attach them
  • One job per prompt — then follow up
  • Talk back — “shorter”, “in Hindi”, “as a table”, “what did you miss?”
  • Let it ask — “Ask me 3 questions before you start”
  • Check two things before you trust the rest

5️⃣ Generative AI vs Agentic AI (6 min)

▼

Generative AI — you ask, it creates

You give a prompt; it gives back text, a table, an image, code. Every step after that is yours: you check it, you send it, you act.

Agentic AI — you give a goal, it takes steps

It plans, uses tools (opens files, searches, updates a sheet, sends a draft), checks its own work and reports back — within limits you set. It acts in the world, so it needs permissions and approvals.

A spectrum, not a switch:

Chat
answers questions
→
Chat + tools
reads files, searches, calculates
→
Automation
fixed steps someone designed
→
Agent
decides the steps itself

What changes when AI can act

GenerativeAgentic
Who actsYouThe system — with your approval
Main riskA wrong answerA wrong action (an email sent, a file changed)
SafeguardsCheck before useLimited permissions, approval steps, logs
Where Suroj isToday's sessionPhase 2 and 3 — built with your teams
🎤 Trainer: Use the swap-table agent for your session. End with: “Everything today is generative. The previews at the end of the session show where agents come in.”

6️⃣ What AI Can and Can't Do (7 min)

▼
🎯 What we are trying to achieve

Build the instinct for when to use AI, when to check it and when not to use it.

📦 What happens

Vote on twelve real tasks, then reveal.

🗳️ Use it, check it, or don't — vote, then reveal

Summarise a 40-page document into one page
Excellent at it — but check it didn't drop the one clause that matters.
Translate a site notice into Hindi and Marathi
Strong — have a native speaker glance at it before printing.
Draft a polite reminder email
Ideal job. You still press Send.
Total a 2,000-row cost sheet in its head
Ask for code or a formula instead.
Tell you the latest GST rate change
Its knowledge stops at a date — use search mode and confirm on the official source.
Decide whether to bid on a tender
A business decision with accountability. AI can prepare the facts; people decide.
Turn messy notes into a table
One of its best uses.
Count sleeves on a photographed drawing
Reads text on drawings well; counts symbols badly. Count yourself.
Write an Excel formula
Fast — test it on three rows you know.
Decide which worker to dismiss
Decisions about people need human judgement, fairness and accountability.
Explain an unfamiliar term (e.g. CPI, EMD)
A patient tutor. Ask for an example from construction.
Cite a court case or IS code clause for a claim
Classic hallucination risk — open the source before using it.

When confident text went out unchecked

  • Lawyers, New York, 2023 (Mata v. Avianca): filed a brief citing court cases ChatGPT had invented. The court sanctioned them.
  • Air Canada, 2024: its website chatbot told a customer about a refund policy that didn't exist. A tribunal held the airline responsible for what its chatbot said.
  • Deloitte Australia, 2025: a report for a government department was found to contain references that didn't exist; the firm agreed to refund part of its fee.

The common thread: the AI wasn't punished. The people and companies who sent it were.

7️⃣ Safe and Responsible Use (6 min)

▼

What may go into an AI tool

TierExamplesFree personal app?
PUBLICGeneral questions, published standards, training data like today'sYes
INTERNALYour own notes with names removed, templates, general process descriptionsOnly anonymised
CONFIDENTIALClient documents and drawings, prices, budgets, margins, contracts, salariesNo — company-approved accounts only
NEVERPasswords, OTPs, bank details, Aadhaar/PAN, firewall or system configurationsNever, in any AI tool

What happened elsewhere

  • Samsung, 2023: engineers pasted internal source code into ChatGPT to debug it; the company then restricted generative AI use.
  • Arup, 2024: an employee in Hong Kong joined a video call with deepfaked senior colleagues and transferred about US$25 million to fraudsters.

AI also makes fraud more convincing: verify any payment or password request by calling back on a number you already have.

Personal data

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 puts obligations on how organisations handle people's personal data. Workers' names, phone numbers, Aadhaar, salaries and attendance are personal data — they don't go into personal AI apps.

Ten rules for the card on your desk

  1. Use the company-approved account for company work.
  2. Turn off “improve the model” / training on personal accounts.
  3. Never paste passwords, OTPs, bank or ID numbers.
  4. Remove names and figures before using a personal app.
  5. Ask for sources — and open them.
  6. Check numbers by calculation, not by trust.
  7. AI drafts; you decide and sign.
  8. No decisions about people by AI alone.
  9. Be careful with others' copyrighted material and drawings.
  10. Unsure? Ask EDP before you paste.
🎤 Trainer: For Session 4, hand this module to an EDP participant for 60 seconds — rules land better from IT than from the trainer.

⚡ Brain Break 1: Know Suroj & the Tender Desk

▼
⏱ 4 minutes · Icebreaker · Read the question aloud, take a show of hands, then tap an answer

1. For which client did Suroj build the aircraft manufacturing facility in Nagpur?

A is correct. DRAL's leadership credits Suroj on suroj.in. Project references like this are exactly what PQ criteria ask for.

2. In a tender, “EMD” stands for:

C is correct. The bid security. Wrong amount, wrong form or short validity is a common reason bids are rejected.

3. When the GCC and the SCC say different things, which usually prevails?

A is correct. Special conditions modify the general ones. Today's tender says so in 2.7 and 7.0 — check the order of precedence clause in every tender.

4. In an EPC tender, who usually carries design responsibility?

B is correct. That's why EPC bids carry design risk an item-rate bid doesn't — the reason EPC leads Lab 3 today.

📱 Prompt makeover — 5 minutes

Every table · uses the tender PDF
  1. Attach the tender and send: “Summarise this tender.”
  2. New chat, attach again, send the five-part prompt below.
  3. Compare: which one found both bid dates? Which one can you check?
PROMPT — THE MAKEOVER
You are a senior tendering engineer at an Indian EPC contractor. From the attached SYNTHETIC tender, extract into a table (Item | Value | Clause no.): tender issue date, site visit, pre-bid query deadline, pre-bid meeting, bid submission date and time, bid opening, EMD amount and form, bid validity, completion period, estimated cost. If two clauses give different values, show both rows. If something is missing, write NOT FOUND. No commentary.

🧪 Data Lab 1: Read & Qualify — Can We Bid?

▼
🎯 What we are trying to achieve

Decide whether Suroj can bid: pin down the real dates, EMD and bid validity, and test every eligibility criterion against our own project record.

📦 What your table produces

A one-line GO / NO-GO / GO-WITH-ACTIONS with an evidence table, plus the tender conflicts to raise as pre-bid queries.

📂 Files for Lab 1
📄 KLS_Tender_EPC_041_SYNTHETIC.pdf PDF📄 4_Capability_Projects.csv CSV📄 4b_Capability_Profile.csv CSV📄 1_Tender_Clauses.csv CSV

Download to attach in your AI app, or Open to look first.

⏱ 15 minutes · Tender PDF + 4_Capability_Projects + 4b_Capability_Profile · led by Tendering

The situation

Before anyone prices a single item: what are the real dates, how much EMD, how long must the bid stay valid, and does Suroj meet the PQ? The tender says some of these things twice — differently. And the project list has four projects that will look like they qualify.

🪜 Steps to get it done

  1. Download or preview the files above (buttons in the blue box).
  2. Driver attaches the tender PDF and sends Prompt 1 (key terms).
  3. Checker opens two of the clauses the AI cited and confirms them; note every conflict.
  4. Attach the two capability files and send Prompt 2 — eligibility, route by route.
  5. Challenger sends Prompt 3: are any projects counted that shouldn't be? Are certificates valid on the bid date?
  6. Writer writes the go / no-go line with the document actions needed.
PROMPT 1 — KEY TERMS
You are a senior tendering engineer at an Indian EPC contractor. From the attached SYNTHETIC tender, make a table: Item | Value | Clause no. for bid submission date and time, pre-bid query deadline, site visit, EMD (amount and form), bid validity, completion period. Where two clauses give different values, list both and mark CONFLICT. If not stated, write NOT FOUND.
PROMPT 2 — ELIGIBILITY
Using Section 3 of the tender and the attached SYNTHETIC capability files (projects and company profile), check Suroj against each criterion 3.1–3.7. For 3.2, test routes (a), (b) and (c) separately with the INR thresholds (80% / 50% / 40% of INR 48 crore), the completion window (on or after 01-Oct-2019) and the definition of "similar work". Table: Criterion | Required | Suroj's evidence | Met / Not met / Action needed. Then one line: GO, NO-GO or GO WITH ACTIONS.
PROMPT 3 — THE TRAP CHECK
Which projects in the list might look like they qualify under 3.2 but do not? For each, say exactly why (date, sector, value or status). Then check: will every certificate in clauses 3.5 and 3.6 still be valid on the bid date?

✅ Check it — before you trust it

  • ▸ Open both clauses of one conflict the AI reported. Do they really disagree?
  • ▸ Take the largest pharma project on the list. When was it completed — inside the window?
  • ▸ Each certificate's expiry or issue date vs the bid date.
💡 Say this: pre-bid queries close at 17:00 today. Every conflict you found in this lab becomes a query in Lab 3.

Verdict: GO via route (b) — PR-11 + PR-15 — subject to renewing ISO 45001 and a fresh solvency certificate. The most common AI mistake: route (a) with PR-07.

🎯 What we are trying to achieve

The situation

Prashant's point from the call: the risk is in the GCC and SCC. The SCC here quietly rewrites the money terms of the GCC — and adds four risks the GCC never mentions. One SCC clause looks like a change and isn't.

🪜 Steps to get it done

  1. Download or preview the files above (buttons in the blue box).
  2. Send Prompt 1 — GCC and SCC side by side.
  3. Checker reads one clause the AI rated High, and its GCC twin.
  4. Challenger: did the AI flag any SCC clause that actually changes nothing? Take it out.
  5. Send Prompt 2 — money at risk; recompute one figure on a calculator.
  6. Writer sends Prompt 3 — the note to the bid committee.
PROMPT 1 — GCC VS SCC
You are a contracts manager for an Indian EPC contractor. In the attached SYNTHETIC tender, compare Section 6 (GCC) with Section 7 (SCC). Table: Topic | GCC position (clause) | SCC position (clause) | Better or worse for the contractor | Severity (High/Medium/Low). Include SCC clauses that add obligations with no GCC equivalent. Note which prevails (see 2.7 and 7.0). If an SCC clause changes nothing, say so.
PROMPT 2 — MONEY AT RISK
On an estimated contract price of INR 48 crore, quantify in INR crore or days: maximum LD under GCC vs SCC; retention held and for how long; days from RA bill submission to payment; mobilisation advance lost. Show the working for each.
PROMPT 3 — THE NOTE TO THE BID COMMITTEE
Write a 150-word note to Suroj's bid committee: the five most serious contract risks in order, the money or time attached to each, and what we should seek in pre-bid queries. Cite clause numbers. No legal conclusions — flag for legal review.

✅ Check it — before you trust it

  • ▸ Pick one SCC clause the AI rated High. Read it and its GCC twin.
  • ▸ Recompute one money figure on the calculator.
  • ▸ Did the AI flag any SCC clause that doesn't actually change anything?
⚠️ Watch for: AI reading Section 6 first and reporting a GCC term as applicable when the SCC has replaced it. Ask it every time: “does any SCC clause modify this?”

⏱ 3 minutes · After Lab 3 · Read the question aloud, take a show of hands, then tap an answer

1. GCC 6.18 gives price variation; SCC 7.6 says firm price. What applies?

D is correct. The single most expensive miss in this tender.

2. PR-07 is a pharma project worth INR 41.2 cr. Why doesn't it qualify?

B is correct. Read the window, not just the value.

3. SCC 7.10 on performance security:

C is correct. The trap. Flagging it as a risk costs points.

B is correct. Open-ended scope in a lump sum is exactly what pre-bid queries are for.

✨ Phase 2 Preview: The Tender Command Centre

▼
Open on the projector: claude.ai/artifact/CudEv6vQPKqQmhuRFbHQW3

Why this works as the closer

For 70 minutes the room has worked one tender with prompts and checking — and knows every trap in it. Now they see the same tender as one screen: the countdown, the conflicts, GO-with-actions, money at risk, Annexure-Q ready to send, interface gaps, BOQ benchmark, pipeline pulse. Then they ask it questions, live. The contrast is the pitch — no slides needed.

Run-sheet — 14 minutes

MinShowSay
0–2Top strip“This is the tender you've been reading since 11. Pre-bid queries close at five. Here's everything you found — in one screen.”
2–4GO — with 2 actions“Your Lab 1 answer, with the evidence. PR-07 isn't counted — the screen knows the window.”
4–6Contract risk tab“INR 14.4 crore at risk or tied up. Tap any clause — it opens. The PBG row says TRAP.”
6–8Pre-bid queries tab“16 queries in Annexure-Q. Copy, paste, send before five. Compare with your Lab 3 list.”

14–16Phase 1 → Phase 2“Today: you plus prompts, one tender, 70 minutes. Phase 2: every tender, on arrival, on Suroj's own data, inside Suroj's approved environment. What stays human: go/no-go, price, every word that goes to the client.”
⚠️ Be honest about what it is. It's a preview built on today's synthetic tender, not a product Suroj can switch on tomorrow. If the network fails, the three suggested questions have prepared answers.

📚 Reserve Case File: When Confident Text Goes Out Unchecked

▼

GLOBAL Deloitte Australia — a government report with invented references

▼

What happened

In 2025 a report Deloitte delivered to an Australian government department was found to contain references that didn't exist and a misattributed court quotation; generative AI had been used in preparing it.

Lesson for the tender desk

A technical submission or deviation schedule that cites a clause, standard or project that isn't real costs credibility with an evaluator — permanently. Every reference is checked.

🗣️ Discuss · 2 min

Which documents leave the tender desk with references in them? Who checks them today?

SUROJ SCENARIO The summary that missed the SCC

▼

Scenario

A busy week. An engineer asks a chat app to “summarise the commercial terms” of a 900-page tender and forwards the summary. It reports price variation on steel — from the GCC. The SCC, 600 pages later, made the price firm. The app had silently stopped reading.

Lesson

Split by section; ask “does any SCC clause modify this?”; demand clause numbers.

🗣️ Discuss · 2 min

What would have caught it before the bid price was fixed?
